heading: 1680 to 1795 — Database of Alcohol Pachters at the Cape of Good Hope
text: 1680 to 1795 — Database of Alcohol Pachters at the Cape of Good Hope
html: 1680 to 1795 — Database of Alcohol Pachters at the Cape of Good Hope

text: Alcohol, whatever form it may take, played an important part in not only the diet (which was more limited in its choice of drinks), but also the recreational life of people of all ranks in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, arguably even more than today. This was also the case at the Cape of Good Hope where, since its inception in 1652 as a halfway station between the Netherlands and the Dutch East Indies, people of European descent brought their culture of consumption with them, which eventually also came to be that of the slaves and Khoikhoi (though not without some reciprocal influences).
html: Alcohol, whatever form it may take, played an important part in not only the diet (which was more limited in its choice of drinks), but also the recreational life of people of all ranks in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, arguably even more than today. This was also the case at the Cape of Good Hope where, since its inception in 1652 as a halfway station between the Netherlands and the Dutch East Indies, people of European descent brought their culture of consumption with them, which eventually also came to be that of the slaves and Khoikhoi (though not without some reciprocal influences).

text: How, however, was the consumption and distribution of alcohol to be managed and controlled? The model was based on that of Europe, and so within four years after the foundation of the halfway station at the Cape, some free burghers were allowed to open inns. During the next 10 years several other individuals ran some sort of tavern or informal inn, while the Council of Policy (hence: CP) was continually besieged by free burghers who wanted a concession to open an inn or a tavern. Since the Cape was run by the VOC who had the monopoly over everything, nobody could start an inn or a tavern without their permission (not that this prevented smuggling). At first the inn and tavern keepers did not have to pay for their concessions, but they had to buy all their stock from the Company and had to sell everything at prices fixed by the Company.
html: How, however, was the consumption and distribution of alcohol to be managed and controlled? The model was based on that of Europe, and so within four years after the foundation of the halfway station at the Cape, some free burghers were allowed to open inns. During the next 10 years several other individuals ran some sort of tavern or informal inn, while the Council of Policy (hence: CP) was continually besieged by free burghers who wanted a concession to open an inn or a tavern. Since the Cape was run by the VOC who had the monopoly over everything, nobody could start an inn or a tavern without their permission (not that this prevented smuggling). At first the inn and tavern keepers did not have to pay for their concessions, but they had to buy all their stock from the Company and had to sell everything at prices fixed by the Company.

text: This situation of haphazardly giving individuals the right to sell alcohol in small quantities soon changed, primarily because of the difficulty in controlling smuggling and because of the enormous profits that the privileged inn and tavern keepers made. In 1665 the CP instituted a system of liquor licences. Only those who were awarded a licence could sell liquor in small quantities to the public. These licence holders did not (at first) have to pay for their licences, but had to buy all their wine and liquor from the Company and had to pay various excises for different types of alcohol. It was the CP which decided whom would be awarded licences (i.e. it was not open to anyone). Mostly it was a small group of people whose licences were continually renewed. However, this system soon began to change, primarily because of the growth in alcohol production at the Cape (especially wine production) and the subsequent growth of the alcohol trade during the 1670s. The company started to charge a fee for some of the licences and in 1674 allowed Jacob Rosendael to open a wine shop on the condition that he pays a set amount for this ‘privilege’ every year. This idea, i.e. to pay the Company for the right to sell a certain type of alcohol, is at the heart of the pacht system.

In 1665 the CP instituted a system of liquor licences. Only those who were awarded a licence could sell liquor in small quantities to the public. These licence holders did not (at first) have to pay for their licences, but had to buy all their wine and liquor from the Company and had to pay various excises for different types of alcohol. It was the CP which decided whom would be awarded licences (i.e. it was not open to anyone). Mostly it was a small group of people whose licences were continually renewed. However, this system soon began to change, primarily because of the growth in alcohol production at the Cape (especially wine production) and the subsequent growth of the alcohol trade during the 1670s. The company started to charge a fee for some of the licences and in 1674 allowed Jacob Rosendael to open a wine shop on the condition that he pays a set amount for this ‘privilege’ every year. This idea, i.e. to pay the Company for the right to sell a certain type of alcohol, is at the heart of the pacht system.

text: However, the system of liquor licences caused a great deal of discontentment among the free burghers since it in effect meant that only a very small group of people benefited from the profitable alcohol trade. This, together with the ever growing illegal trade in alcohol, and all the problems concomitant with it, resulted in various visiting VOC commissioners instituting several reforms in the regulations for and management of the alcohol trade during the 1670s. Thus in 1673 it was decided to auction off four licences every year. However, this was something of a sham, as the CP would only allow those they deemed ‘fit’ to bid for a licence – in effect not changing anything. Yet, change did come in 1679 when commissioner Dircq Blom drew up proper pacht contracts and two of the alcohol pachten were auctioned off publicly (even though the CP still drew up a list of only 8 people who were allowed to bid). The success of this first ‘public’ auction (it brought in more money than the Company ever got in one year from the liquor licences), made the CP decide to lease out (‘verpachten’) most of the food and drink trade in various ‘pachten’ (i.e. leases) and to sell them every year at a public auction to the highest bidder who could also produce two sureties. In principle everyone who could afford it, could become a pachter.

Yet, change did come in 1679 when commissioner Dircq Blom drew up proper pacht contracts and two of the alcohol pachten were auctioned off publicly (even though the CP still drew up a list of only 8 people who were allowed to bid). The success of this first ‘public’ auction (it brought in more money than the Company ever got in one year from the liquor licences), made the CP decide to lease out (‘verpachten’) most of the food and drink trade in various ‘pachten’ (i.e. leases) and to sell them every year at a public auction to the highest bidder who could also produce two sureties. In principle everyone who could afford it, could become a pachter.

text: While a wide variety of edible commodities was leased out over the years, it was the alcohol pachten which were the most spectacularly successful, and which stayed quite stable during the 18th century, in effect becoming the corner stone of the commercial life at the Cape. There were however some changes made to them over time, and hence some background is needed to understand the various alcohol pachten.
html: While a wide variety of edible commodities was leased out over the years, it was the alcohol pachten which were the most spectacularly successful, and which stayed quite stable during the 18th century, in effect becoming the corner stone of the commercial life at the Cape. There were however some changes made to them over time, and hence some background is needed to understand the various alcohol pachten.

text: During the 1660s and 1670s a trend developed to differentiate between the various sorts of alcohol that a specific licence holder was allowed to sell. As a result of this, different licences were instituted for a specific type or a group of closely related types of alcohol. Thus, at the inception of the pacht system in 1679/80 there were four different alcohol pachten, viz. Cape malt beer, brandy, Cape wines and one which included European beers and wines. In the early eighteenth century the rights to sell certain types of alcohol in Rondebosch and in Stellenbosch and Drakenstein were also auctioned off as pachten. In the second half of the century another new alcohol pacht appeared, viz. the right to provide wine and other liquors to foreign ships visiting the Cape. Thus, at the height of the system there were seven different alcohol pachten. (Please note that at first the pachten were auctioned off on the last day of the calendar year, and therefore ran from 1 January to 31 December. This changed in 1698 when the pacht year only ran from January to the end of August. From that year onwards the pacht year coincided with the VOC’s financial year: 1 September to 31 August. Thus, any date after 1699 in this database should be interpreted as a pacht year, i.e. running from 1 September of the previous calendar year until 31 August of the stated year). Some notes on them in the order that they were auctioned off each year (and with the abbreviations used in the database):

Some notes on them in the order that they were auctioned off each year (and with the abbreviations used in the database):

text: This pacht was not auctioned off with the other alcohol pachten on 30 December 1679, but was included from the next year onwards. Because this pacht often remained in the same hands (the pachter was also the brewer) for a long time, it was sometimes not auctioned off publicly, but instead a specific arrangement was made between the CP and the incumbent pachter to pay some set price for it yearly. Where two people shared the pacht during the same year, this is indicated by a ½-sign after that year. This pacht was not awarded in 1720.  BW: Brandewijnen

BW: Brandewijnen

text: This pacht also included the right to sell aracq and distilled spirits, and from 1696 Spanish wine and secq (a heavy Spanish wine) too. From the 1704 pacht year onwards this pacht was divided into four parts (‘percelen’), each auctioned off separately. Thus for every year there are four different contracts. However, there was no limit on how many parts any individual may buy, and hence some individuals held several parts or even all in a given year. In the database, as in the contracts, I indicate which of the four parts a pachter bought (in brackets after the given year).

From the 1704 pacht year onwards this pacht was divided into four parts (‘percelen’), each auctioned off separately. Thus for every year there are four different contracts. However, there was no limit on how many parts any individual may buy, and hence some individuals held several parts or even all in a given year. In the database, as in the contracts, I indicate which of the four parts a pachter bought (in brackets after the given year).

text: This pacht’s name changed a few times, but it more or less always gave the right to sell Dutch (‘vaderlandsche’) and other European (‘uijtheemsche’) beers and wines, i.e. not the Cape varieties for which separate pachten existed. This pacht was not awarded in 1714.
html: This pacht’s name changed a few times, but it more or less always gave the right to sell Dutch (‘vaderlandsche’) and other European (‘uijtheemsche’) beers and wines, i.e. not the Cape varieties for which separate pachten existed. This pacht was not awarded in 1714.

text: Eventually the most valuable of all the pachten, this pacht had a troublesome start and a complex development. Because of various problems, especially a shortage of wine in the early 1680s, the privileged licence holders’ contracts were continually renewed (and they were given all sorts of discounts). This pacht was only auctioned off with the other three alcohol pachten at the end of 1683. From 1700 onwards the pacht was divided into four parts, and like the brandewijnen pacht, each part was auctioned off separately. In the database this is indicated with numbers (1, 2, 3, 4) following the given year. In 1706 W. A. van der Stel tried to institute a ‘generale (wijn) pacht’ – i.e. one person bought the whole pacht at a higher price than the four parts combined. However, the following year the usual format was resumed which lasted until 1735 from which date a ‘generale pacht’ was instituted again. After 1735 there are therefore no numbers after the stated year, except on three occasions (1759, 1794-1795) when there were no ‘generale pachters’ and the four individual pachters together held the wine pacht. Having said all this, in some years two (or even three) people bid together for the ‘generale pacht’ and they therefore shared the wine pacht between them. This is indicated with a ½-sign after the year in which there were two partners, and a ?-sign for three partners. Finally note that the pachters for 1711 held the pacht for only 11 months.

text: All the above pachten were limited geographically to ‘this Table Valley’, usually giving the farm Roodebloem (modern Woodstock) as the boundary. The Company’s farm Rustenburg was rented out to private individuals during 1673-1683 and not only produced wine for the Cape market, but seemingly also sold some in the area. However, the farm reverted to the VOC, but in 1716 (the pacht year 1717) it was decided to institute the Rustenburg pacht, after the example of the Stellenbosch pacht (see below). This basically meant the right to sell various sorts of alcohol in the area beyond Table Valley (but did not include renting the farm). At first it was called the Rustenburg pacht, but from 1721 the Rondebosje. In 1744 the area was extended to also include Baaij Fals (i.e. Simonstown).

text: In 1714 a pacht was instituted for Stellenbosch and a year later for Drakenstein. The pachten gave the pachters the right to sell wine and brandy in small quantities within the boundaries of the district. Up to 1722 they were auctioned off separately and had different pachters. From 1723 onwards, they were amalgamated into one pacht which gave the pachter the right to sell in both areas. For the period before this the abbreviations S and D are used in the database to designate Stellenbosch and Drakenstein.

text: This curious pacht was only instituted in 1757 but soon came to be extremely valuable. The Company levied excise duties on all alcohol sold to ships of foreign nations docking in Table Bay. The right to manage and collect this excise became the seventh of the alcohol pachten. This pacht was not awarded in 1783 and 1784.

text: The aim of this database is to present alphabetically all the individuals who held any alcohol pacht, with a cursory indication of which pacht(en) he or she held when, during the period 1680-1795.  The year 1680 was chosen as a start as this is the year in which the major characteristics of the pacht system were established (as described in paragraph 1), even though not all the pachten were publicly auctioned off in that year.

text: The list is filed alphabetically according to surname. Under each name the pachten the person held are given in the order they appear above and using the same abbreviations as in paragraph 2. After identifying the pacht, only the year(s) during which the individual held that specific pacht is given with no further information. After the name of every person who held pachten in more than one year, a date is given (in italics) of the first and the last year in which they held any pacht. This is to show the period of the given pachter’s activities. Please note: Before 1698 the year given refers to the calendar year from 1 January to 31 December. 1698 only refers to 1 January to 31 August. From 1699 onwards, any given year refers to the period from 1 September of the previous calendar year until 31 August of the stated year. Thus, for example, the year 1702 should be interpreted as 1 September 1701 to 31 August 1702.

text: I have followed the modern Afrikaans (and not the Dutch) usage of filing surnames starting with van, le or de under those words, and not the under the main word, e.g. van der Spuij is filed under van, not Spuij. I have consistently used the grapheme ij not y, but treated it as a y, i.e. it is filed between x and z.
html: I have followed the modern Afrikaans (and not the Dutch) usage of filing surnames starting with van, le or de under those words, and not the under the main word, e.g. van der Spuij is filed under van, not Spuij. I have consistently used the grapheme ij not y, but treated it as a y, i.e. it is filed between x and z.

text: As with all sources from the 17th and 18th centuries, there is very little consistency in the spelling of proper nouns. I have been guided by the form used most often, and have mostly, but not always, changed it where necessary in accordance with the spelling used in the register to H. C. V. Leibbrandt’s Requesten (Memorials). Cross references have, however, been included to facilitate searching. Names in which patronyms appear have been filed under the last name, i.e. the surname, though cross references to the patronyms have been included. Thus, Jan Dirkz de Beer is filed under de Beer. In cases where toponyms are used as surnames, e.g. Michiel van Lijpsigh, they were filed under van. Where toponyms appear after a surname, they have been placed in brackets, and the person’s name filed under the surname, e.g. Jan Rogiers (van Amsterdam) is filed under Rogiers. Women’s names, where possible, have been filed under their maiden names, though cross filings under their married names are included. In cases where the correct name has not been ascertained, the only reference is to the married name with the addition of widow or wife. Where part of a name is in brackets it means that that part is sometimes given as part of the person’s name, but otherwise often omitted. For example: Hurter, (Jan) Willem means that the person mostly appears under the name Willem Hurter, but also occasionally as Jan Willem Hurter.
html: As with all sources from the 17th and 18th centuries, there is very little consistency in the spelling of proper nouns. I have been guided by the form used most often, and have mostly, but not always, changed it where necessary in accordance with the spelling used in the register to H. C. V. Leibbrandt’s Requesten (Memorials). Cross references have, however, been included to facilitate searching. Names in which patronyms appear have been filed under the last name, i.e. the surname, though cross references to the patronyms have been included. Thus, Jan Dirkz de Beer is filed under de Beer. In cases where toponyms are used as surnames, e.g. Michiel van Lijpsigh, they were filed under van. Where toponyms appear after a surname, they have been placed in brackets, and the person’s name filed under the surname, e.g. Jan Rogiers (van Amsterdam) is filed under Rogiers. Women’s names, where possible, have been filed under their maiden names, though cross filings under their married names are included. In cases where the correct name has not been ascertained, the only reference is to the married name with the addition of widow or wife. Where part of a name is in brackets it means that that part is sometimes given as part of the person’s name, but otherwise often omitted. For example: Hurter, (Jan) Willem means that the person mostly appears under the name Willem Hurter, but also occasionally as Jan Willem Hurter.
